page0.text:
It's the middle of the night, but the church is brightly lit.
Saber hands the unconscious victim over to me in front of the church, and I take her inside.
I call loudly for Kotomine, who comes out, takes one look at the victim, and carries her into a back room.
Apparently, the only room that's usable as a treatment room is Kotomine's own chambers.

page1.text:
"Haah..."
I sit on one of the pews.
...For now, I've done everything I can.
It's up to Kotomine whether she'll pull through.
I just have to trust him and wait for the outcome.

page2.text:
...
...Time passes.
I know Saber's waiting for me outside, but I can't leave just yet.

page3.text:
Besides, I want some time to think alone.
The Matou family turned out to be a bloodline of mages.
Shinji became a Master with a Servant under his command.
Zouken Matou let the family heir fight in the Holy Grail War, even though they've lost their power.

page4.text:
"..."
The Einzberns aren't the only faction with a fixation on the Holy Grail.
Makiri and Tohsaka.
In fact, people close to the grail itself are bound to become Masters.

page5.text:
...Even Saber is no exception.
The Einzberns sought the grail for a thousand years.
I can't even begin to imagine that level of obsession.
There are things that require the Holy Grail's power to be saved or healed.

page6.text:
My old man defied the grail and chose to destroy it instead.
Can I see this through to the end with the same conviction?
Do I really have the right to fight in the same war as the Einzberns and Makiris,
who have been chasing their goal for hundreds of years...?

page7.text:
"I must say, I didn't expect you to bring me an injured person the very same day I offered to help you."
"Kotomine."
I look up.
Kotomine's expression isn't grim.
That must mean the treatment went well.

page8.text:
"Kotomine, what happened to the woman?"
"I've done what I can. The rest depends on her. If you'd brought her even a half hour later, I would have had to perform the rites of my actual occupation."

page9.text:
"...I see. Sorry, and thanks.
I'm...glad you were awake."
"What's wrong? Does it pain you so much to express gratitude to me? If anything troubles you, I'll listen."

page10.text: "...I dunno. I've got plenty on my plate right now, and you're the one who keeps adding to it. I'm sick of hearing your long sermons."

page11.text:
"Our discussion today bothered you? ...Hm. I meant to motivate you, but it seems to have only confused you further. That's quite regrettable."
The priest seems rueful, but I can't tell how sincere he is.

page12.text:
"..."
But I'm not going to let this awkward silence win.
"So, um...
Someone I know is a Master."
I murmur pitifully, unable to keep it to myself.

page13.text:
The priest says nothing.
He merely nods in acknowledgement.

page14.text:
"And you defeated him, of course."
I answer the short question with a nod of my own.

page15.text:
"Then there is no need to be sorry. People cannot change their pasts.
All we can do is affirm our own actions.
If you must shoulder your sins, then question your next actions. Only you can decide how to face the tragedies of the past."

page16.text:
"..."
The priest is right, again.
The problem isn't that Shinji was a Master, or that the Matou and Tohsaka families are mages, or that the Einzberns are obsessed with the Holy Grail.
What matters are the choices I make next.

page17.text:
"I'm going home. Take care of her."
I stand up and make to leave the chapel.
Saber's waiting for me outside.
Now that I know the woman will be all right, I have no reason to stay here.

page18.text:
"A moment, Shirou Emiya. Allow me to offer a word of advice."
"...What now? I already said no more lectures."
"It won't take long. I've already gone through the trouble of healing your charge in the middle of the night, so consider this your fee and listen."
"..."
Can't argue with that.
I reluctantly turn back and stand in front of the priest.

page19.text:
"I neglected to mention something today.
The Einzberns have survived for the last millennium in pursuit of their wish. It's quite a monumental feat, and you were only right to feel daunted by it."
"..."
...This is why I can't deal with this guy.
I haven't even said anything yet, but he hits me right where I'm most uncertain.

page20.text: "...You're so annoying. Are you still going on about that?"

page21.text:
"That's not my point. I'm merely saying that you needn't overly concern yourself with it.
It isn't anything extraordinary. It's quite a common circumstance in this war, actually.
The Holy Grail War is a crystallization of man's feats and blessings. One need not feel guilt in joining the war, nor killing over it."

page22.text:
"All humans have their respective wishes and compete to fulfill them. That is what life is all about. Whether great or small, we all share in this underlying principle.
I doubt you will ever find an exception to this rule.
Of course, success and failure are a different matter. While we all live in pursuit of our objectives, we all meet our ends without ever reaching our goals."

page23.text:
"All things have an order to them. A wish can only be fulfilled through sufficient effort and resources. We call that accumulated vain effort 'life.'
The Holy Grail simply abridges that necessary effort.
And the Holy Grail War is a mortal battle to simplify the human way of life."

page24.text:
"In other words, it is nothing special.
The seven Masters are simply attempting to take the shortest path to achieve something that otherwise would have taken their entire lives to do.
But there's nothing else particularly extraordinary about it. It's utterly human for people to crush others' wishes to make their own come true.
The Holy Grail War is no different from life itself.
You should simply do as you desire and win, without troubling yourself over it."

page25.text:
"..."
The priest's tone is pleasant.
To him, there's no difference between noble and mundane wishes.
He doesn't judge the quality of anyone's desire.
He's saying I should follow my heart and trample on everyone else's wishes...
I can't tell if he's being sarcastic or not.
But what I hear loud and clear is his serious declaration that even a half-baked Master like me can find meaning in this war.

page26.text:
"...Hell must have frozen over, if you're worrying about me."
"Oh, I simply told you not to worry. After all, I'd be a failure of a priest if I added to my flock's troubles, instead of lifting them away."
...What a piece of work.
If Tohsaka heard that, she'd say he's always been a failure.

page27.text:
"I never asked for that. See you around, fake priest."
"Yes. Do fail to learn your lesson and come again."
I snort, turn on my heel, and march out of the church.
This time, I really do leave, announcing it with loud and forceful footsteps.

page28.text:
Saber's waiting for me outside the church.
...Come to think of it, my daytime visit went exactly like this, too.
Saber patiently waited for me in the frigid winter night.

page29.text:
That might be how a Master-Servant dynamic is meant to be anyway, but she's still here for my sake.
I hope I can repay her goodwill.

page30.text:
"She's going to be all right. It's all thanks to you, Saber."
"I require no thanks. You're the one who saved that woman, Shirou. I merely accepted your decision."
"Ngh..."
She gives me a surprisingly kind expression.

page31.text: "Ah, um...that's not true. You saved her. I never would have made it in time, plus..."

page32.text:
She let Zouken Matou get away, just to help a victim.
If we'd stopped the old man from leaving, there would have been another fight. The woman was in critical condition, and wouldn't have made it.
Saber must have had that in mind when she let Zouken go.

page33.text:
"W-what is it, Shirou? You're smiling for no reason."
"Huh? Oh, there's a good reason. I'm glad you lived up to first impressions. Thank you, Saber. I'm happy that you went along with my stupid orders."

page34.text: "S-speak nothing of it! I would never defy your—"

page35.text:
"Oh really, now? I seem to recall you calling me naïve and soft, saying that I don't know what war is like.
Saber, your face said that you'd do your best to cooperate but would change the plan if the situation called for it."

page36.text:
"N-no I wasn't! I simply said that I would prioritize my own decisions if you were in danger! Don't give me that tone, Shirou!"
Saber grunts in indignance.

page37.text:
...
Her pouty face looks so similar yet different from the way she's been acting that I can't help but smile.

page38.text:
"Shirou. It appears that you need a lesson in manners."
"Then you'd better teach me once you get a chance. But more importantly, we should end this war."

page39.text:
"Shirou?"
"Unlike you, I don't need the Holy Grail.
I was thinking that we'd end the war and give the Grail to you if we survive. I wasn't confident that my half-hearted conviction made me good enough to be your partner, Saber."

page40.text: "I see. And now? You engaged in battle of your own accord. Have you had a change of heart?"

page41.text:
"Not at all. I still don't accept this Holy Grail War.
...But, I'll fight until the end.
I don't have a wish for the Holy Grail, unlike the others.
But my objective has always been to protect other people. To do what's right.
That doesn't mean I think any less of the others. They all have their own reasons for fighting. Some have been after the Grail for five hundred years or even a thousand."

page42.text: "I see. Yes, that does make sense."

page43.text:
"Then allow me to swear an oath to you.
As long you are worthy of my service, I swear to be your sword. Remain true to yourself, Shirou...and I will never betray you."
"Ah...Yeah. I'll do my best, Saber."

page44.text:
Her honest smile makes me feel a little awkward, so I look up at the sky.
The starry winter sky reminds me of a frozen lake. It's so beautiful.
